newsitem.title: MEXICO: COFFEE-Mexican business unveils beans-to-cup plan.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE-Mexican business unveils beans-to-cup plan.

text.p: Mexican coffee farmers are being offered a beans-to-cup integrated support project this 1996-1997 cycle in a revolutionary bid to revitalise the cash-strapped sector.

The Mexico City-based Union de Credito Para La Eficiencia Empresarial, a loan company and farm consultancy, is currently pulling together $20 million in global credit lines to finance its visionary project that offers finance, technical and trading support to growers.

Project Coordinator Ignacio Luyando said the integrated plan intends this cycle to sign up 200 producers or producer groups, with a strong focus on co-operative participation, especially from indian and organic growers.

He recognises the $20 million in credits is a small start for a country that has exported a record 4.6 million 60-kilo bags worth over $663 million in the 1995-1996 cycle but he is confident of its success.

"We know the $20 million will be fully taken up, but we do not want to stretch ourselves in this first cycle," Luyando said, adding the idea is a Mexican modification of similar schemes operating in countries such as Colombia.

Three foreign banks and one Mexican bank are in line to provide the credits that will be backed by coffee. "We will take out put options to assure a minimum price that will cover the credits," Luyando said.

"Coffee is the source of payment so we have to assure that it is of the best quality and produced at the lowest possible cost," Luyando added, explaining the theory behind the technical support and trading support the company will give to coffee growers who enter the financial programme.

Alongside the finance, the company, known as UCEE from its Spanish intials, has a three-pronged assistance approach focusing on giving growers technical advice, coffee trading back-up and access to coffee market information.
On the technical side, UCEE is offering on-plantation site advice to growers, traveling workshops and updates from investigation centres on new advances in disease and frost resisitant varieties.
Help to sell coffee focuses on several fronts.

That includes cutting costs in terms of bulk buying of raw materials, such as fertilizers, coffee certification to obtain higher gradings, and coffee trading services help, such as contracting customs agents, insurance and transportation.

"We are also setting up a trading unit to sell coffee direct," Luyando said, adding the company would offer warehousing services up to 10 months so growers had the option to sit on stocks and wait for price spikes.
"Retail banks just do not want to know the agricultural sector," said Puebla coffee grower Jose Manuel Toscana, who intends to sign up in the integrated project.

"This is a visionary plan that will help us catch up from decades of being left in the wilderness compared to other countries," he added. "My fertilizer costs are going to go down by 30 percent, for example, that is a great saving."

Coffee growers around the country have shown interest. They include groups in the Tapachula, Motozintla and Yajalon areas of Chiapas state, Cordoba, Huatusco and Coatepec growers in Veracruz, Pluma Hidalgo, Huatulco and Nopala producers in Oaxaca state, Atoyac Coffee growers in Guerrero state and growers from Xicotepec and Cuetzalan in Puebla state, Luyando said.
"Soon other grower groups in the states of Nayarit, Jalisco and Colima will also be invited to take part," Luyando said.

The scheme, seen with certain reserve by established Mexican coffee traders and exporters because it could over time eat into their traditional markets, has been received well by the Mexican Coffee Council, the government-private sector umbrella organization that promotes Mexican beans.
"We have told the council what we are doing and they are all in favour," Luyando added.
